quarterly.title: AI Pulse
quarterly.subtitle: Where AI growth is speeding up and where it is slowing, across the AI supply chain.
quarterly.tagline: Shows where growth is speeding up or slowing across the AI supply chain.

notes.growth: Growth compares sales (or spending, or exports) with the same period a year earlier: the latest quarter for companies that report quarterly, the last 3 months for monthly data. Speeding up or slowing compares that growth with the reading three months earlier. Whether a change counts as speeding up depends on how fast the part already grows: a few points is a lot for a slow grower and little for one growing several-fold. A part needs most of its companies moving the same way, so a part whose companies are split reads steady. Each part's growth is its typical (middle) company or trade figure, not the industry total.
notes.guide: Outlooks are the companies' own sales forecasts for next quarter, turned into growth on the same quarter a year earlier. For big tech's data-centre spending it is the full-year spending plan.
notes.market: Share price vs chip stocks is a company's share price over the last 3 months against SMH, a fund that holds the big chip stocks, in US dollars. It is price, not sales, and counts in no status.
notes.dates: Every number carries the date it was public by (for monthly data, the filing deadline or the day this page first saw it).
notes.census: This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.

overview.lead: More than half of AI's parts (8 of 13) are growing faster than three months ago. Memory is speeding up the most.

Microsoft's 2026 spending plan was said on its call and reported by the press; it has no earlier plan to compare with.
Oracle's fiscal 2027 spending plan has no number yet ("higher than fiscal 2026").
The history uses today's figures with the dates they first came out; later revisions are not undone.
US memory-chip imports are small and swing a lot, so they count in their parts but stay out of the biggest-moves lists.

fast.title: AI Pulse: this week
fast.subtitle: Faster readings for the same parts of the AI supply chain: share prices, foreign buying in Taiwan, the newest export figures and GPU rental prices, and interest (what people read, search for and talk about).

notes.what: The quarterly picture moves when companies report. These readings move every day or every week, so a change shows up sooner.
notes.status: A part reads SPEEDING UP only when different kinds of fast readings agree on the way up and few point down, SLOWING the other way round, and STEADY otherwise. A part with a single reading gets no word. The arrows show each reading on its own.
notes.attention: Interest puts together what people read on Wikipedia, what builders talk about on Hacker News and, once they arrive, Google searches and news coverage. It counts as one reading however many places it comes from. The Wikipedia arrow shows whether reading, measured against a year earlier, is growing faster or more slowly than a couple of months ago. Wikipedia reading of most AI and chip topics speeds up and slows down together, so many parts slowing there at once is mostly one story: interest in AI and chips in general growing more slowly.
notes.ai_use: AI use looks at AI assistants and AI search themselves (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and others): Wikipedia reading of their pages today, open-model downloads from late November, Google searches once they arrive. It is shown on its own and does not count toward any part.
notes.dates: Every number carries the date it was public. Asian closes count on their own date, before the US open of that day.
notes.weeks: Weeks before Oct 5, 2026 are rebuilt from share prices, interest (Wikipedia reading and Hacker News talk, the two kinds with a long record) and Korea's export counts only; the other readings have no earlier record. A kind of interest joins the weeks from the day it has figures.
